summary: The disaster bigger than your government: {the disaster} is past what {the place} can handle, and help from {higher government} comes with a question of who is in charge.
realLife: One life: Before Hurricane Katrina in 2005 the Louisiana governor asked the president in writing for help. She declined his offer to federalize the state's National Guard, accepted responsibility for state failures after he accepted federal blame, and in 2007 called for an inquiry into whether partisan politics slowed the response. Another: In California's 2001 electricity crisis the federal administration refused to step in, and the state bought power itself. Another: In January 2013 he attacked his own party's House Speaker for delaying a vote on hurricane aid.
gates: {the disaster} is on record in your place.
You can ask {higher government} for help.
weights: Whether {higher government}'s leader is of your party.
choices: ask early, in writing, for everything
refuse to hand over command of your own forces
accept the blame for your part

branches.then: You refuse in writing to keep your powers, and the standoff is the story for weeks.
You are left to make costly deals on your own (C19).
You accept your part too, and the blame stays with you longer than with them.
Months later few have been paid. You call for an investigation into whether party politics slowed the help.

branches.when: your own party's leaders delay the aid
